items.title: Sweeping Anti-Conversion Law Leads Indian Churches to Cancel Vacation Bible Schools
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Whoa.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Churches in the Indian state of Maharashtra are reportedly cancelling Bible camps during Diwali, a Hindu holiday celebrated during the autumn season, because of a recently enacted anti-conversion law.

For context, Maharashtra is India’s second most-populous state and includes Mumbai, the largest city in the country. Only about 2.3% of India’s 28 million people identify as Christians, making believers an extreme minority in the nation.

Much like in the U.S., the Bible camps — vacation Bible schools — last several days and consist of music, games and competitions, and stories and lessons based on Scripture, all for children ranging in ages from five to 15 years old. In India, they typically take place in the fall, according to Premier Christian News.

Some area churches, though, have cancelled their planned VBS events altogether, while others have restricted it strictly to Christian kids — a shift from the typical strategy of using the Bible camps as opportunities to evangelize.

It all comes down to Maharashtra’s sweeping Freedom of Religion Act, signed into law by Indian President Droupadi Murmu on July 30 and enacted the following month. The language of the bill is so broad, critics are concerned it will result in the penalization of Christians and churches. The law states violators may face up to seven years in prison for the non-bailable offense.

The new law bans conversion by “allurement,” a vague and overly generalized term that includes “any temptation in the form of … any gift, gratification, easy money or material benefit either in cash or kind.” It also disallows the offer of employment, “free education in school or college run by any religious body or institution,” a “better lifestyle,” “portraying practice, rituals and ceremonies or, any integral part of a religion in a detrimental way vis-a-vis another religion,” or even “glorifying one religion” — in this case, Christianity — over another.

Additionally, anyone who intends to convert from one religion to another is required to give notice to a governmental authority 60 days prior “to such proposed conversion.” At that point, the official will announce the impending conversion to the involved parties, “calling for objections within [30] days from issuance of notice,” according to the law.

“If any objections are received or otherwise, the competent authority [government official] may make an enquiry through police with regard to the intention, purpose or cause of the proposed conversion,” the bill states, noting that, if a violation is suspected, an investigation will ensue.

According to Premier, at least 12 other states in India have similar anti-conversion laws and, while advocates argue the bills protect vulnerable people from exploitation, others see them as a clear attack on Christian evangelism. The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, for example, has said the laws disproportionately affect Christians and Muslims, and have noted terms like “allurement” are intentionally ambiguous and problematic.

The churches moving ahead with planned VBS initiatives are requiring registration and charging entree fees of 50 to 100 rupees (roughly $1) as a way to prove parents sent their children to these faith-based camps intentionally and of their own accord.

items.title: Evangelist Claims Police Threatened to Arrest Him For Preaching Jesus at Christmas Festival
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "Blatantly unconstitutional."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Evangelist David Hoffman is pushing back after he says police demanded he go to a “remote speech zone” while sharing the Gospel during a holiday festival last year in Tucson, Arizona.

First Liberty, a First Amendment legal advocacy firm, is taking on his case and pushing back against what it calls “open hostility to religious speech” that is “blatantly unconstitutional.”

Attorney Garrett Bell sent a demand letter asking the city to step back, arguing that what happened at the Winterhaven Festival of Lights was improper.

“I run an outreach and evangelism ministry called Kingdom Enterprises,” Hoffman told CBN News. “We do U.S.-based street ministry and evangelism. We’re based in Tucson, Arizona, and … there’s a winter event that we have traditionally gone to pretty much every year over the past 10 years — except for COVID — and we go, and we have conversations with people.”

The team hands out Gospel tracts and shares about Jesus. He said this became a problem in 2025, when they went to the event, and police officers approached them before they were fully set up.

“Police approached us, and they told us that, if we continued within the event, we would be ticketed and arrested,” Hoffman said.

Hoffman recalled asking the police questions and said cops affirmed they had the authority to arrest him, which left him concerned about continuing to push back. So, he listened to the authorities and went to the free speech zone. Then, he later reached out to First Liberty.

Bell said this alleged interaction amounted to censorship, adding that the push to send people to supposed “free speech zones” is deeply problematic.

“We like to just call it a ‘designated speech area,’ because there’s nothing free about it,” Bell said. “They’re largely unconstitutional.”

Bell said it was also troubling that Hoffman had been to the event many times before without incident, and added that this was the first year festival organizers received a permit from the city of Tucson that included this free speech policy — one purportedly dictating that there could be “no religious messaging or materials distributed.”

“You have to be in this designated speech area, and that area is outside of the main footprint of the event,” Bell said. “And it’s sort of this small, confined, barricaded space where Hoffman and his group were pretty well separated from anyone they really wanted to reach.”

The entire ordeal left Hoffman shocked, because he said the event is public. In his view, the suggestion he and his group should be disallowed is wrong.

Bell filed a complaint and a motion for preliminary injunction, but the first step they took was to send a demand letter to the city.

“To this day, they [have] not responded [to our letter] and, because the Winterhaven Festival is right around the corner for 2026, we filed that complaint and preliminary injunction,” Hoffman said. “And, as of now, have not received an answer or response from the city.”

CBN News will continue to cover the story as it unfolds. A request for comment from the city has not been returned.

items.title: Sadie Robertson Huff Was the Poster Child for Christianity. She Says It Nearly Crushed Her.
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: “The pressure of that felt so crippling because I wasn’t living that way,” she says of being cast as the model Christian girl on Duck Dynasty. It led to her keeping God at a distance whenever she struggled, until one night when “a freight train of God’s grace” hit her.
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

By her teens, Sadie Robertson Huff had been cast as something she never auditioned for. Huff grew up on camera, on A&E’s Duck Dynasty, in a family that lived its faith out loud, and viewers took the teenager at the center of it as the model Christian girl. She says she felt every bit of that expectation.

“I was put in this position to be this poster child for Christianity,” she said. “I’m in this Christian family. They’re all living boldly for their faith. I need to be this good example. And yet the pressure of that felt so crippling because I wasn’t living that way.”

The gap between the image and the girl got filled with performance. Huff says she kept showing viewers the version they wanted.

“Instead of just being honest and being vulnerable and being authentic and saying I struggle, I was trying to be what people were projecting on me.”

That began to change with her first YouTube video. She posted it with wet hair and no makeup, which was a bigger statement then than it sounds now, and told viewers they had it wrong.

“Hey, I’m Sadie Robertson, and here’s what my life looks like. A lot of you guys keep saying I’m goals, but I’m really struggling. I feel really insecure. I have a lot of anxiety.”

It was the first time she let the audience see the person underneath. The poster-child pressure had followed her into her prayer life, though.

“I felt like I had to be perfect for him to be proud of me. I had to be perfect to stay in right relationship. And when I wasn’t perfect, because no one is, and I definitely struggled a whole lot, then I would just distance myself from him. When you’re struggling, that’s when you need to draw near. But when I’m struggling, I’m like, ‘I gotta get it together so that I can come near.'”

The video changed how she showed up online. The private version came later, after she had kids. She was behind at work, exhausted and sure she was failing at all of it. One night, after putting the children to bed, she went outside to tell God she was sorry she just couldn’t keep up.

“I walked outside to have some quiet time, and it was like a freight train of God’s grace hit me. I had no anticipation of feeling weight lifted. I had all the anticipation for repentance. I was going to say, ‘Lord, I’m dropping the ball in every area.’ And yet I sat there and I just felt God’s embrace and I just cried. I came back in to my husband and I said, ‘That was the craziest experience. I thought He was gonna be mad at me, but He just loved me.'”

She admits it sounds hard to explain. “I can’t explain it other than it was like an embrace,” she says. “I just felt a weight lifted.” Since then she’s been on a mission to tell people that God is more gracious, more kind and more loving than they think.

Huff keeps returning to the woman at the well to explain what happened to her. She has heard John 4 preached all her life, she says, and rereading it, she noticed what the woman chose to say when she ran back to town.

“Come meet a man who told me everything I ever did. That was the testimony. And that revelation of this man knows me, and he was willing to sit with me, and he was willing to drink from my cup, that he actually loves me.”

Her new book, It’s Not Personal, is built on the same story.

The comparison has a Christian version, too. Huff says she and her husband guard against it.

“One thing as a culture we have created in the Church sometimes is that competitive spirit of who gave the best message at the conference, who did the best worship set. Christian and I are like, we cannot let our mind go there. Don’t pay that attention, because it does something to your heart. Then you’re striving. I gotta bring my best. It’s gotta be better than I was last year.”

The expectations that came with being a poster child have not gone away. Every time Huff has been in what she calls the storms of social media, she says, the criticism has come from the Church, never from the secular world. When criticism from fellow Christians piled up online, including over a TikTok dance, she dreaded the next Sunday.

“I felt nervous to go to my church, because I felt like everybody’s seen this on Facebook, everybody’s seen this on Instagram and TikTok, and I just didn’t want to feel eyes on me,” she said. “I felt sad about it, I felt hurt by it. And so Christian and I were like, ‘Hey, it’s okay. We just need to go.’

“I was trying to slip out to go help one of my kids, and one of the elders just walked up to me and said, ‘Hey, I just want to encourage you. God is using you in such a mighty way.’ He didn’t bring up the controversy. I’m sure he saw it, based off of just how kind he was being, but he just spoke so much truth in my life. And I just was thinking, I’m so grateful that I came to church.”

She says she never wants to bash the Church. She’s had hate from it and so much love, she says, and she believes in it deeply. Her request is for the people who treat the internet as a separate place.

“We all have social media. I’m seeing you react to me. I’m scrolling, it’s in my algorithm. And so don’t take the humanity out of people on the other side of the screen. It matters so much that you’re loving them just as much.”

The criticism has also followed a harder question. Huff preaches, and she didn’t grow up in a church that allowed women to. Her family wrestled with it before she said yes, she says, reading through the scriptures and asking big questions, and she is grateful they did. The comments arrive anyway.

“People comment all kinds of stuff. ‘Sit down, shut up, you are feelings based, emotion based.’ I’ve seen the comments. I’ve seen the things. But I go back to what I know to be true and what the Lord has spoken, and what I’ve read and studied and people spoke into my life. It’s hurtful, it’s sad.”

What carries her through it, she says, is something Shelley Giglio once told her.

“Life is gonna be hard, but you’re looking for assurance that it’s what the Lord told you to do. Because if you have assurance, then you’ll be able to get through the hard.”

It is a long way from the girl who believed she had to get it together before she could come near to God.

items.title: Fourth Annual New Ressourcement Conference Highlighted the Works of Joseph Ratzinger
items.author: Word on Fire
items.summary:
Word on Fire
Word on Fire hosted its fourth annual New Ressourcement Conference from November 4–6, 2026. The theme was “Joseph Ratzinger and His Sources,” in honor of the upcoming centenary of Ratzinger’s birth (April 16, 2027). Scholars were invited to share papers reflecting on the minds and texts
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Word on Fire

Word on Fire hosted its fourth annual New Ressourcement Conference from November 4–6, 2026. The theme was “Joseph Ratzinger and His Sources,” in honor of the upcoming centenary of Ratzinger’s birth (April 16, 2027). Scholars were invited to share papers reflecting on the minds and texts that shaped Ratzinger’s writing. 

“Joseph Ratzinger’s theology grew out of a lifetime of reading: Scripture and the liturgy, Augustine and Bonaventure, and the friends, teachers, and opponents he engaged along the way. This year’s conference brought scholars together to study those sources and to ask what they still offer the Church,” said Dr. Jason Paone, director of Word on Fire Academic. “With the centenary of his birth approaching and the inaugural volume of his Collected Works now available in English, this is a good moment to read Ratzinger the way he read the tradition, by going back to the sources.”

The conference included several keynote speakers:

  • Bishop Robert Barron, Diocese of Winona-Rochester: “The Necessity of a Metaphysics of Logos in the Determination of Justice: An Examination of the Ratzinger-Habermas Debate.”
  • Tracey Rowland, University of Notre Dame Australia: “Gottlieb Söhngen: Champion of the Analogia Fidei and its Critical Concepts.”
  • Cyril O’Regan, University of Notre Dame: “Benedict’s Sources: Imitation, Emulation, Figuration.”

The eight plenary speakers were Jennifer N. Martin (University of Notre Dame), Christopher Ruddy (Catholic University of America), Fr. Aaron Pidel (Pontifical Gregorian University), Fr. Maurice Ashley Agbaw-Ebai (Angelicum), Nina Heereman (St. Patrick’s Seminary and University), Fr. Emery de Gaál (University of Saint Mary of the Lake), Pietro Luca Azzaro (Fondazione Ratzinger), and Alejandro Sada (Universidad Panamericana). 

Throughout the conference, more than forty additional papers were shared during concurrent sessions on Scripture, liturgy and the sacraments, the Church Fathers, Bonaventure, philosophy, and Protestant theology.

Select essays will be published in the Fall 2027 special issue of The New Ressourcement journal, guest-edited by Tracey Rowland and Fr. Maurice Agbaw-Ebai.

The conference opened two days after Word on Fire Academic launched Jesus of Nazareth, the inaugural volume of the Joseph Ratzinger: Collected Works, the English edition of his non-magisterial writings.

The fifth annual New Ressourcement Conference will take place from November 16–19, 2027, at The Catholic University of America in Washington, DC. The theme will be announced in the coming months.

items.title: ‘To Be More With Him’: The Poetry of John Paul II
items.author: Lindsey Weishar
items.summary:
Lindsey Weishar

His poetry is a largely untapped source of inspiration with the potential to enrich Catholic arts and literature in profound ways.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Lindsey Weishar

One Easter as a teenager, I received The Place Within: The Poetry of Pope John Paul II. It was probably the most memorable thing I ever found in an Easter basket. Having now spent a number of years with Wojtyła’s poetic voice, I have come to believe his poetry is a largely untapped source of inspiration with the potential to enrich Catholic arts and literature in profound ways.

This is not the first time Pope John Paul II’s poetry has been discussed in this forum. In his October 2022 article “St. John Paul II, the Polish Poet,” Robert Mixa unfolds for readers Wojtyła’s poetic heart and astutely notes, “My concern is that we in the West tend not to associate John Paul II with poetry whereas my experience in talking to Poles who knew John Paul II mostly describe him as an intellectual poet, reading his philosophy and theology as stemming from his poetic heart.”  

Why might it be that for all the ways we’ve explored his encyclicals, letters, and even his plays, we have less familiarity with Wojtyła’s poetry?

George Wiegel notes in Witness to Hope that Wojtyła’s poems are difficult in both Polish and English. Jerzy Pietrkiewicz, translator of Wojtyła’s poetry, gives insight as to why this might be in his introduction to Wojtyła’s Collected Poems: “As regards metre [meter], the important thing to remember is that Polish verse is essentially syllabic; English, by contrast, is stressed. But within the Polish metrical system, Wojtyła’s verse is not at all typical. On the contrary, he shows a marked preference for long lines, some of them very long indeed, eighteen or twenty syllables, not common in Polish prosody.” 

Add to this a poetic style that speaks with and circles back on itself—looking at an idea, concept, or person from multiple viewpoints—and we can understand why the initial approach to Wojtyła’s poetry might leave a reader scratching his head.

Another reason that the approach to Wojtyła’s poetry has perhaps been a bit slower in the West may be because Wojtyła typically published his poems under a pen name in Polish, and the first English translation of his poetry was about fifty years ago.

Active in the intellectual and artistic life as a priest, particularly in his early priesthood, Wojtyła contributed essays to the Catholic literary and intellectual journals Tygodnik Powszechny (Universal Weekly) and Znak (Sign). And it was to these journals that he also submitted his poetry, usually under the pen name Andrzej Jawień and sometimes Stanisław Andrzej Gruda. Wiegel notes that this was perhaps “to make a distinction between his literary work and his writing on religion, faith, morals, and Church affairs, which were always published under his own name.” Wojtyła also wrote, Wiegel reminds us, during a time of heightened political tension when some bishops disapproved of these journals, and the Communist party kept close watch on them. Weigel adds that Wojtyła “thought he had the right to have his work considered on its own merits, rather than as clerical curiosities.”  

Performing Poetry, Meditating on the Word

Wojtyła’s poetic heart found expression not only in written poetry but in poetry expressed theatrically. In Collected Poems, Pietrkiewicz notes that “Wojtyła’s own writing for the theatre favored ‘a many-voiced monologue’ [a term first used by the Polish Romantic poet, Norwid], as if he wished to weld unspoken thoughts to the thoughts already encapsulated in words. A technique of this kind must, by virtue of repetitions or echoes, blur the outlines of direct speech.” Likewise, many of his poems take up a subject like thought or a biblical figure like Simon of Cyrene and examine the multifaceted nature of the subject or person.

Wojtyła’s first direction in life lay in the realms of literature and theater. When he entered college in 1938, he started studying Polish language and literature at the Jagiellonian University. On September 1, 1939, the Nazi invasion of Poland halted his education, so Wojtyła joined actor and theater director Mieczysław Kotlarczyk’s Rhapsodic Theater. As St. John Paul II says in his book Mystery and Gift, this form of theater focused on “the delivery of the poetic text.” Performing poetry was a common choice in this theater group’s repertoire. In a letter written to Kotlarczyk in 1939, Wojtyła expresses his passion for this type of performance: “Being an artist, I am not a sword-wielding man, but I want to build the Polish theatre and poetry, even if for next to nothing, with all my Slavic soul, with all my eagerness and youth, and with my sleeves rolled up.” 

How these Rhapsodic Theater performances looked is somewhat hard to imagine. But amazing things have been done with Wojtyła’s plays. The example of a 2025 performance of Wojtyła’s early play, Jeremiah, at the Angelicum gives us some idea. Wojtyła himself wrote about the elements of the Rhapsodic Theater in a 1952 essay entitled “On the Theater of the Word.” We learn that Rhapsodic performances don’t so much tell a story as unfold an idea. One example is Wojtyła’s poetic play, The Jeweler’s Shop, which meditates on the vocation of marriage. (While it contains a narrative, greater room is given to contemplating human love, as a line from Act III shows: “In the Bridegroom’s face each of us finds a similarity to the faces of those with whom love has entangled us on this side of life, of existence. They are all in him.”) Supporting the fact that the spoken word has precedence of place in Rhapsodic Theater, costumes and sets are minimal and movement is dance-like, serving to complement the word. Some parts are spoken collectively as a chorus.

“Reality [Cannot] be Grasped by One Instrument Only”

Theater, for Wojtyła, was one way of interacting with the word and the Word, offering in its embodied performance a particular perspective on reality. Poetry was another. Weigel highlights a point so important to Wojtyła’s worldview: “Reality could not be grasped by one instrument only.” While philosophy certainly has its place, “Literature, in crucial respects, was a more supple instrument for delving into the hidden depths of the human condition.” 

One example of this is that in 1960, both Love and Responsibility and The Jeweler’s Shop were published. One is a philosophical and theological exploration of human love; the other, as has been noted, is a play that explores these themes through story. In a similar vein, in 1999, Pope John Paul II released his “Letter to Artists,” which he opens with the following: 

None can sense more deeply than you artists, ingenious creators of beauty that you are, something of the pathos with which God at the dawn of creation looked upon the work of his hands. A glimmer of that feeling has shone so often in your eyes when . . . you have admired the work of your inspiration, sensing in it some echo of the mystery of creation with which God, the sole creator of all things, has wished in some way to associate you.”

It is likely that John Paul II wrote this letter on the artistic vocation near the time he himself was in the midst of an artistic endeavor—a return to poetry. Accordingly, in 2003, The Poetry of John Paul II, Roman Triptych: Meditations was published. 

Though Wojtyła did not write much poetry during his papacy, his love for language and poetic expression did not diminish. As close friend and author of Discovering the Human Person: In Conversation with John Paul II, Stanisław Grygiel, put it, “But only at the end of his life did he return to the ‘great lady,’ as he called poetry. He reproached himself for not having always remained faithful to her. In Roman Triptych, he immersed himself once again in the ‘torrent of beauty,’ to help us join him in contemplating his own Petrine ministry in the Church.”  

This collection, in a thematic echo of the “Letter to Artists,” begins with a meditation on Genesis and a poem called “Stream.” A few striking lines from this poem follow: 

The running stream cannot marvel,
and silently the woods slope down,
following the rhythm of the stream—
but man can marvel!
The threshold which the world crosses in him
is the threshold of wonderment.
(Once, this very wonder was called “Adam”).

He was alone in his wonder,
among creatures incapable of wonder—
for them it is enough to exist and go their way.
Man went his way with them,
filled with wonder!
But being amazed, he always emerged
from the tide that carried him,
as if saying to everything around him:
“Stop—in me is your harbour”,
“in me is the place of meeting
with the Primordial Word”.
“Stop, this passing has meaning . . .
has meaning . . . has meaning”.

Performing Wojtyła’s Poetry

Inspired by Wojtyła’s performance of poetry in the Rhapsodic Theater, I have become convinced that Wojtyła’s poems are also meant to be performed. The embodied word imparts a life we cannot find from silent reading on the page alone. 

In 2022 and 2024, I gathered a small group to perform Wojtyła’s poem cycle, “Profiles of a Cyrenean.” Published by Tygodnik Powszechny in 1957, the poem is broken into three distinct parts.  
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

Part I explores the Simon of Cyrene, who is in all men, in each of us. As a line from this part of the poem reads, “I know the Cyrenean’s profile best, / from every conceivable point of view.” 

In Part II, different facets of who Simon could have been are explored through fourteen different voices or profiles that range across types of people—“Melancholic,” “Actor,” and “Armaments Factory Worker”—to more abstract inner realities: “Man of Emotion,” “Man of Intellect,” and “Man of Will.” Each voice is occupied with a variation of the same question: “What is my relationship to the cross, to Christ?” “Will I carry the cross?” 

Part III presents the moment in which Simon of Cyrene is taken from the crowd to help carry the cross. Wojtyła takes us into Simon’s thoughts as the drama of this scene unfolds. Simon must decide if he will remain mentally distant from the Lord or if he will allow the Lord to touch his mind and heart.  

Parts I and III were performed in a reader’s theater-style chorus, whereas Part II was performed by individual actors.

As we performed “Profiles” during Lent, each actor was encouraged to pray into their Part II profile throughout the season, to learn the words by heart, and to bring to the performance the fruit of their prayer. Each participant was invited to choose his or her own costume and to interact with our only prop—a wooden cross—as he or she felt moved. We provided the audience with a preparatory introduction in which we invited them into prayer and meditation, almost as you would the Stations of the Cross. We also provided meditation guides, which contained a line or two from each poem alongside questions to bring to prayer. Knowing that the performance might be difficult for our audience to engage with, we invited them to listen for one particular voice or line that spoke to them. After the performance, we stayed to talk with the audience about what they had witnessed. 

These poems ring out with a truth that even today catches me by surprise, and various lines still linger in my thoughts. For example, the Melancholic’s opening line of “I would not carry it [the cross]” and the desire “to be more with Him, / more with Him, not merely with oneself,” resonates deeply with me; while it may be that “our reality is more magnificent than painful,” it also has great burdens from which we’d rather turn away. In the performed word—a word that needs our voices and bodies to enter the world in a comprehensible form—we see, meditate upon, and ultimately, share with others the Word that has inspired our own. 

Wojtyła’s Poetic Legacy

As has been pointed out by Anna Kozłowska in her study of Wojtyła’s poetics, in Mystery and Gift, Wojtyła gives us the key to his love for language: 

The word before it is ever spoken on the stage, is already present in human history as a fundamental dimension of men’s spiritual experience. Ultimately, the mystery of language brings us back to the inscrutable mystery of God himself. As I came to appreciate the power of the word in my literary and linguistic studies, I inevitably drew closer to the mystery of the Word—that Word of which we speak every day in the Angelus: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14)

Karol Wojtyła’s poetry is an invitation to uncover what the “Word made flesh” looks like in our own creative lives. In a world increasingly given over to the intangible, the technological, and the non-human, Wojtyła’s poetry sparkles with life, involving the whole of us. Through reading his poetry and through prayerful performance of it (which I pray will become more customary in the coming years), we are invited to come close enough to ponder, like Simon of Cyrene, Christ’s closeness: “Who is to say which is which / when the weight knocks us both the ground— / me and him?” We are invited to discover him within us like the woman at the well (the focus of another of Wojtyła’s poem cycles) that “His recognition was different . . . / He saw me in himself, possessed me / in himself.” 

Just as the subjects of Wojtyła’s poetry experience the deepening and transformation of perception, we too are called to be changed by the Word. As Rocco Buttiglione highlights in Karol Wojtyła: The Thought of the Man Who Became Pope John Paul II, Wojtyła’s poetry “shows the transformation of hearts, the implacable deepening of authentic personal reality which existence, honestly experienced, imposes.” Through the performance of his poetry, my prayer is that our own eyes, “transfixed more by light than by sorrow,” (to borrow a line from Wojtyła’s poem, “Song of the Brightness of Water”), may be filled by undaunted wonder, that the sorrow that weighs down our world may be met by Christ’s light within us.
